title: Top 10 Essential English Verbs for Absolute Beginners (A0–A1 / A2 Master Guide)
dek: A complete 12-page magazine spread for absolute beginners discovering English. Master the top 10 core verbs step-by-step, starting with a deep dive into the verb 'To Be' with full conjugations, 10 core usage patterns, negative/question structures, and real-world sentence frames.

blocks.text: Page 1: Introduction to the Top 10 Core Verbs

Welcome to Part 1 of our 2-part master verb guide for A0–A1 and A2 English learners! When you start learning English, you don't need thousands of words to start speaking. Frequency research demonstrates that just 10 core verbs carry up to 80% of daily spoken output. This 12-page issue gives every core verb its own dedicated page with clear grammar rules, practical sentence frames, real-world examples, and common traps to avoid.

The verb **to be** is the most foundational verb in English. At A0–A1 level, you use it to talk about who you are, how you feel, where you are, your age, job, nationality, weather, time, and daily states.

rows: I am very happy today. / I'm tired after work.
You are my best friend. / You're on time for class.
He is a doctor at the hospital. / He's tall and funny.
She is at home in the kitchen. / She's a good student.
It is cold outside. / It's 10 o'clock in the morning.
We are ready for the lesson. / We're excited to learn.
They are university students. / They're busy today.

items:
**A. Identity & Names (Subject + be + noun):**
  • *Examples:* Hello, my name **is** Damian, he **is** my brother Alex, Lady Gaga **is** his favourite singer, and they **are** my best friends from school. This **is** my new book.

**B. Jobs & Roles (Subject + be + a/an + job):**
  • *Examples:* I **am** an English teacher, I **am not** a student, and my brother **is** a hospital doctor, so he **is not** an IT specialist. Lady Gaga **is** a famous singer and an actress.
  • ⚠️ **ATTENTION:** Always use **a** or **an** before singular countable jobs (*a doctor*, *an actress*, *an IT specialist*).

**C. Age (Subject + be + age):**
  • *Examples:* I **am** 29 years old today, my younger brother **is** 20 years old, and my parents **are** 55. How old **are** you?
  • ⚠️ **ATTENTION:** In English, we say *"I am 20 years old"* or *"I am 20"*. **NEVER** say *"I have 20 years"*.

**D. Nationality & Origin (Subject + be + nationality / from + country):**
  • *Examples:* I **am** French, I **am not** Italian, and my brother **is** Spanish because our family **is** from Paris. They **are** Italian tourists.

**E. Descriptions & Characteristics (Subject + be + adjective):**
  • *Examples:* My friend Dylan **is** tall and he **is** very funny. The classic movie **is** black and white, and my bedroom **is** clean today. The birthday cake **is** delicious.

**F. Feelings & Physical States (Subject + be + state):**
  • *Examples:* I **am** very happy to meet you, but we **are** extremely hungry and thirsty after work, and Dylan **is** very tired.

**G. Location & Spatial Prepositions (Subject + be + location):**
  • *Examples:* Today I **am** at home, my brother **is** in the kitchen, my keys **are** on the wooden table, and my colleagues **are** at work.
  • *Key Prepositions:* **in** (in the room), **on** (on the table), **under** (under the bed), **next to** (next to the café), **behind** (behind the house), **in front of** (in front of the school), **between** (between two shops), **near** (near the station), **at** (at work/school).

**H. Time, Weather, and Dates (It + is + time/weather/date):**
  • *Examples:* It **is** Friday morning, and it **is** 11 o'clock. The weather **is** sunny but it **is** cold outside. Today **is** October 23.

**I. Demonstratives & Possession (This/That is, These/Those are):**
  • *Examples:* This **is** my leather bag, that **is** her younger sister, these **are** our study books, and those people **are** my parents.
  • ⚠️ **IMPORTANT:** *To be* identifies who something belongs to (*"This bag is mine"* / *"This is my car"*). It does not replace *have* (*"I have a car"*).

**J. Material, Measurements & Numbers:**
  • *Examples:* This dining table **is** made of solid wood, the total price **is** €10, the subway station **is** 2 kilometres away, and my room **is** 4 metres wide.

blocks.text: To make a negative sentence, add **not** after *am*, *is*, or *are*.

rows: I am not tired after sleep. / I'm not a French student.
He isn't at home right now. / She isn't at school. / It isn't expensive.
We aren't late for class. / You aren't wrong about time. / They aren't hungry.

blocks.text:
⚠️ **IMPORTANT NEGATIVE RULES:**
• Say **I am not** or **I'm not**. There is **NO** form such as "I amn't".
• **DO NOT** use *don't* or *doesn't* with *to be*. Correct: *She isn't happy.* Incorrect: *She doesn't be happy.*
To ask a question, invert the subject and *am / is / are*.

rows: Is she at home this afternoon?
Are they ready for the lesson?

blocks.text: ⚠️ **SHORT ANSWER RULE:** In positive short answers, **never** use contractions. Correct: *"Yes, she is."* Incorrect: *"Yes, she's."*

items: **What:** *What is your full name?* / *What is this object on the desk?*
**Who:** *Who is she?* / *Who are those people over there?*
**Where:** *Where are you right now?* / *Where is my smartphone?*
**When:** *When is your birthday party?*
**Why:** *Why are you so sad today?* / *Why is he angry?*
**How:** *How are you feeling today?* / *How are your parents?*
**How old:** *How old is your younger brother?* — *He is 18 years old.*
**How much:** *How much is this blue leather bag?* — *It is €20.*

**What... like?:** *What is your new teacher like?* — *He is friendly and funny.* (Asks about character/description).
  • *Note:* Contrast with *How is your grandfather?* — *He is fine today.* (Asks about health/well-being).

blocks.text: 6. Essential Structures & Daily Expressions with "To Be"

items:
**A. There is / There are (Existence):**
  • Singular: *There is a white cat in the garden.* / *There isn't a free chair here.* / *Is there a bank near here?*
  • Plural: *There are two chairs in the kitchen.* / *There aren't any students in class.* / *Are there any open shops?*

**B. Essential Fixed Expressions with "To Be":**
  • *be right / be wrong:* You are right about the answer, but I am wrong.
  • *be afraid / be sure:* She is afraid of dogs, but I am sure everything is fine.
  • *be interested in / be good at:* He is interested in modern music, and I am good at English.
  • *be late / be early / be ready / be busy / be free:* We are late for work, dinner is ready, and I am free tomorrow.

blocks.question: Choose the correct form: 'She ___ 25 years old and she ___ a doctor.'
blocks.explanation: In English, we use 'to be' for age ('She is 25') and for professions ('she is a doctor'). Never use 'has' for age.

blocks.question: Is she at home? — Choose the correct positive short answer:
blocks.explanation: In positive short answers, never use contractions. Always use the full form: 'Yes, she is.'

blocks.text: The verb **to have** is one of the most essential verbs in English. At A0–A1 level, you use it to talk about possessions, family, physical characteristics, food and drink, daily activities, health conditions, and obligations.

There are two essential present simple forms to learn first:
• **have** — I, you, we, they
• **has** — he, she, it

⚠️ **IMPORTANT CONJUGATION RULE:** Use **has** only with *he*, *she*, and *it* in positive present simple sentences.
• Correct: *She has a cat.*
• Incorrect: *She have a cat.*

items: **A. Possessions:** *I have a new laptop.* / *She has a red bicycle.* / *We have a big house in Paris.* / *They have a friendly dog.*
**B. Family & Relationships:** *I have two brothers.* / *She has a young daughter.* / *He has a big family.* / *We have many good friends.*
**C. Physical Characteristics:** *I have brown eyes.* / *She has long blonde hair.* / *He has a dark beard.* / *The cat has a long tail.*
**D. Things & Features:** *The apartment has three bedrooms.* / *The car has four doors.* / *My phone has a great camera.* / *The school has a large library.*
**E. Problems & Needs:** *I have a problem with my laptop.* / *She has a bad headache.* / *We have an urgent question.* / *He has a lot of work today.*
**F. Time & Availability:** *I have free time this afternoon.* / *We have an important meeting today.* / *She has an English lesson at 10 AM.* / *They have no money.*

**G. Food & Drink (Action Meaning):** *I have a delicious sandwich for lunch.* / *She has a cup of tea every morning.* / *We have breakfast at 8 o'clock.* / *They have dinner together at home.* (Here *have* means *eat* or *drink*).

blocks.text: 3. Negative Sentences (-) & The Base Verb Rule
To make negative sentences with *have*, use **don't have** or **doesn't have**.

rows: I don't have any money. / We don't have class today.
She doesn't have a brother. / My phone doesn't have a good camera.

blocks.text:
⚠️ **VERY IMPORTANT RULE:** After *doesn't*, always use the base form **have**, never *has*.
• Correct: *She doesn't have a car.*
• Incorrect: *She doesn't has a car.*

⚠️ **QUESTION RULE:** When you use *does*, the main verb returns to its basic infinitive form, **have**.
• Correct: *Does she have a cat?*
• Incorrect: *Does she has a cat?*

items: **What:** *What do you have in your bag?* / *What do you have for breakfast?*
**Who:** *Who do you have in your family?*
**How many:** *How many brothers do you have?* / *How many bedrooms does the house have?*
**How much:** *How much money do you have?* / *How much time do we have?*
**What colour:** *What colour eyes does she have?*
**What kind:** *What kind of phone does he have?*

blocks.text: *Have got* is common in informal English (especially British English) for possession, family, and physical features.

rows: I have a car. / She has a cat.
I've got a car. / She's got a cat.
I don't have a dog. / She doesn't have a car.
I haven't got a dog. / She hasn't got a car.
Do you have a pet? / Does she have a car?
Have you got a pet? / Has she got a car?
Yes, I do. / No, she doesn't.
Yes, I have. / No, she hasn't.

blocks.text:
⚠️ **NEVER MIX THE TWO SYSTEMS:**
• Correct: *Does she have a car?* OR *Has she got a car?*
• Incorrect: *Does she have got a car?*

items: **Daily Activities & Routines:** *have breakfast / lunch / dinner*, *have a coffee*, *have a shower / bath*, *have a break*, *have a rest*, *have a party*, *have a good time*, *have a look*, *have a chat*, *have a holiday*.
**Illnesses & Physical Conditions:** *have a headache*, *have a stomachache*, *have a cold*, *have a fever*, *have a toothache*.

**Countable vs Uncountable (some / any):**
  • Affirmative (+): *I have some apples.* / *I have some water.*
  • Negative (-): *I don't have any apples.* / *I don't have any money.*
  • Question (?): *Do you have any questions?*

blocks.text: Use **have to / has to + base verb** to express obligations and necessary actions.

items: **Affirmative (+):** *I have to study for the exam.* / *She has to work tomorrow morning.* / *We have to clean the house.*
**Negative (-):** *I don't have to work today.* (It is not necessary, but permitted). / *She doesn't have to cook dinner.*
**Question (?):** *Do you have to wear a uniform at school?* / *What time does he have to leave?*

blocks.text:
Contrast these four key structures with 'to be' and 'to have':
• **State / Feeling:** *I am hungry.* (be + adjective)
• **Possession:** *I have a sandwich.* (have + noun)
• **Activity:** *I have breakfast at 8 AM.* (have + meal)
• **Necessity:** *I have to eat something.* (have to + base verb)

blocks.question: Choose the correct negative form: 'She ___ a brother.'
blocks.explanation: After 'doesn't', the main verb always returns to its base form 'have'. 'She doesn't have a brother' is correct.

blocks.question: Which sentence correctly mixes 'have got' and 'do'?
options: Does she have got a car?
blocks.explanation: Never mix 'do/does' with 'got'. Use 'Has she got a car?' or 'Does she have a car?'

blocks.text: **To Think** allows you to express your opinion, share your thoughts, and ask others for their view.

items: **Present Simple Forms:** I/You/We/They **think** | He/She/It **thinks**.
**Expressing Opinions (I think that...):** *I think it is a good idea.* / *I think learning English is fun.* / *She thinks this movie is great.*
**Short Responses:** *I think so.* (I agree / I believe so) | *I don't think so.* (I disagree).
**Asking Opinions:** *What do you think about this idea?* / *What do you think of this film?*
**Key Collocations:** *think twice before deciding* (be careful), *think about the problem* (consider), *think of a solution* (have an opinion/idea).

blocks.text: **To Know** is used for facts, familiarity with people/places, and skills (*know how to*).

items: **Present Simple Forms:** I/You/We/They **know** | He/She/It **knows**.
**Knowing Facts:** *I know the right answer.* / *I don't know the address.* / *She knows where the keys are.*
**Familiarity (People & Places):** *Do you know Paul from work?* / *I know this historic city very well.*
**Skills & Abilities (know how to + verb):** *I know how to drive a car.* / *She knows how to cook delicious Italian pasta.*
**Useful Daily Expressions:** *Let me know when you arrive* (inform me), *As far as I know, the shop is open* (to my knowledge), *You know...* (filler phrase).

blocks.text: **To Like** expresses preferences, tastes, enjoyment, and polite offers (*would like*).

items: **Present Simple Forms:** I/You/We/They **like** | He/She/It **likes**.
**Like + Noun:** *I like hot coffee in the morning.* / *She likes outdoor sports.* / *Do you like classical music?*
**Like + Verb-ing:** *I like reading books in bed.* / *He likes swimming in the sea.*
**Polite Requests & Offers (Would like):** *I would like a cup of green tea, please.* / *Would you like to join us for dinner?*
**Appearance & Resemblance (look like):** *He looks like his father.* / *What does your new house look like?*

blocks.text: **To Want** and **Would Like** express desires, intentions, and polite requests.

items: **Direct Desires (Want + Noun / Verb):** *I want a glass of cold water.* / *I want to learn English fluently.* / *Where do you want to go tonight?*
**Polite Standard (Would like + Noun / Verb):** *I would like to order lunch now, please.* / *She would like a fresh salad.*
**Negative Forms:** *I don't want to be late for class.* / *He doesn't want to go home yet.*
**Common Phrases:** *if you want to come*, *I want to know the truth*, *we would like to see the museum*.

blocks.text: Page 8: Verb 7 — "To Go / Be Going To"
**To Go** expresses movement, travel, routines, and future intentions (*be going to*).

items: **Present Simple Forms:** I/You/We/They **go** | He/She/It **goes**.
**Movement & Prepositions:** *I go to work by train.* / *She goes to school every morning.* / *We go to the park on Sundays.*
**Exceptions without 'to':** *go home*, *go abroad on holiday*, *go downtown*, *go grocery shopping*.
**Future Intentions (be going to + verb):** *I am going to eat dinner with friends.* / *They are going to buy a new car next month.*
**Transport Phrases:** *go on foot* (walk), *go by bus*, *go by train*, *go by car*.

blocks.text: **Can** is a modal verb expressing ability, permission, and polite requests.

items: **Modal Rule:** *Can* never changes form (no '-s' for he/she/it). It is followed directly by a base verb without 'to'.
**Ability:** *I can speak three languages.* / *She can swim very fast in the pool.* / *He can play the acoustic guitar.*
**Negative Ability (cannot / can't):** *I can't drive a manual car.* / *She can't come to the party tonight.*
**Requests & Permission:** *Can you help me with this bag?* / *Can I have a glass of water?* / *You can sit here near the window.*
**Useful Phrases:** *as fast as I can*, *I can do it*, *Can I ask a quick question?*

blocks.text: **To Eat** is used for food, daily meals, dining habits, and food preferences.

items: **Present Simple Forms:** I/You/We/They **eat** | He/She/It **eats**.
**Daily Food:** *I eat fresh fruit every morning for breakfast.* / *He eats lunch at 1 o'clock at work.*
**Questions & Desires:** *What do you want to eat for dinner?* / *Do you eat vegetarian food?*
**Phrasal Verbs & Collocations:** *eat out at an Italian restaurant*, *eat healthy food*, *let's find something to eat*.

blocks.text: **To Drink** covers beverages, hydration, offering drinks, and social café situations.

items: **Present Simple Forms:** I/You/We/They **drink** | He/She/It **drinks**.
**Daily Beverages:** *I drink two litres of water every day.* / *He drinks black coffee in the morning.* / *We drink hot tea in winter.*
**Offers & Polite Phrases:** *Would you like something to drink?* / *What would you like to drink with your meal?*
**Noun Usage:** *a hot drink on a cold day*, *a cold drink in summer*, *let's have a drink together*.

blocks.text: Grammar & Structure Summary for A0–A1 / A2 Learners

• **Simple Sentence Structures:** Always maintain clear Subject + Verb + Object order.
• **Auxiliaries & Modals:** Use 'can' for ability and 'would like' for polite requests.
• **Full Conjugations:** Explore full present, past, and future conjugation tables across all 14 languages on [COSYtools](https://cosylanguages.github.io/COSYtools/).

📌 Test your skills on [COSYpractice](https://cosylanguages.github.io/COSYpractice/), read [Part 2](top-10-verbs-part-2-en.html) for the next 10 core verbs, and consult full verb conjugations on [COSYtools](https://cosylanguages.github.io/COSYtools/).
